name: reject-alg-substituted
description: An unlock request an issuer must refuse whole: the publisher's own signed resource behind a header that says alg "none". THE ATTACK. The payload segment is the publisher's, byte for byte the one in seal-ecdh.json. The header in front of it was rewritten to {"alg":"none","typ":"JWT","kid":...}, keeping the kid, and the third segment is empty, which is what that algorithm means: there is nothing to check. The blobs, the periodKeys section are the render's own. WHY IT IS NOT THE FORGERY AGAIN. reject-forged-resourcejwt and reject-tampered-resourcejwt both name ES256 and both fail an honest ECDSA verify, so an implementation that pins the key and pins the bytes and takes the algorithm from the header refuses both of them and accepts this one. The header selects WHICH check runs, and it is the check an implementation forgets to make: the key and the bytes are checked by code somebody wrote, the algorithm by code nobody did. WHAT IT BUYS. An accepted token is a payload the attacker wrote - any renderId, and any claim an access decision reads. With the renderId chosen, every sealed blob the attacker holds is presented at a coordinate whose binding the issuer rebuilds from that same chosen renderId, so it opens: the relabel, the cross-render lift and the unknown name in this directory are all refused by a value that is only unguessable while the envelope holding it is. This body is the least version of that - only the header moved, so an implementation that reads it answers 200 with the whole render. A CONFORMANT ISSUER answers 400 with bad_alg. The algorithm is a string comparison against a constant and it comes before the key is fetched, so the refusal costs no signature verification, no ECDH and no key-store lookup - expected.privateKeyReached is false, and a replay that can count operations should see zero of all three. NOT CONFORMANT: reading this payload at all, whatever is done with it afterwards. substitution.alg is the header this arm names. Its sibling reject-alg-substituted-hs256 names a check the issuer can genuinely run, which is the arm that survives a "none" special case. NOTHING IN THIS rawBody MOVES BETWEEN RUNS: there is no ECDSA signature in it, so the exception the other reject vectors make for the third segment does not apply here. REPLAY. Post `rawBody` VERBATIM - the string as it sits in this file, never a re-serialization of it - to the unlock endpoint, with `issuer` as the key material the issuer holds for its own name and keyId, and `publisher.signingKeys` as the public verification halves, read straight from this file rather than resolved by a deployment lookup. A pass is: expected.code where there is one; key material back for exactly the coordinates in expected.keys and no others; and an error back for exactly the coordinates in expected.errors, under the codes recorded there. No publisher private key is in this file, on purpose: an issuer never holds one, so everything a reject vector asks for is checkable with what a real issuer has. HOW FAR THE REFUSAL REACHES IS PART OF WHAT IS PINNED, and expected.privateKeyReached says which side of the line this body lands on. A request that fails integrity - a signature that does not verify, a signed resource with no renderId to bind to - has asked nothing that could be answered, so it is refused whole and before the key store is consulted at all. A blob presented at a coordinate it was not sealed at is one bad blob in an ordinary request: the only way to find out is to try it, so the key store is reached, the blob comes back as an error, and everything else the request carried is answered beside it. The untouched coordinates were never the attack, and a page has to keep working around one bad blob, so they are answered. Everything in the body but the attack is the render this vector was cut from - the envelope, the periodKeys section and the untouched blobs are what the publisher emitted. An unchanged regeneration retains the valid resourceJWT signature segment inside rawBody, so the body is byte-stable with seal-ecdh.json. A fresh seal still draws a new k, which is why a replayer verifies the segment rather than comparing it. The token is the one in the base vector from the same run, byte for byte, except in reject-no-renderid, reject-renderid-noncanonical and reject-renderid-wrong-width, whose envelopes are second tokens signed over resources with the renderId removed, given a noncanonical spelling, or resized, which is each vector's whole subject; in reject-forged-resourcejwt, whose signature segment was drawn by a key the publisher does not hold; in reject-tampered-resourcejwt, which carries the seal-ecdh token's own signature segment under a payload edited after signing; and in the two reject-alg-substituted arms, which carry that token's payload segment under a header rewritten to name another algorithm, with a third segment that is empty or a MAC - neither of which moves between runs.
